LCDC SICAP Regional Workshop - Tipperary
Left to Right: Catherine O Hara, Administrative Officer Rural and 
Community Development Clare County Council, Maria Farry, 
Manager, Programme Development Unit (SICAP/LEADER), Pobal, 
Deirdre Kelly, Principal Officer, Social Inclusion and Communities Unit, 
Department of Rural & Community Development and the Gaeltacht. 
Stephen Walsh, IFA Clare LCDC, Frank Cullinan Staff Officer Rural 
and Community Development Clare County Council, Juan Carlos 
Azzopardi: Development Coordinator, Programme Development Unit 
(SICAP/LEADER), Pobal.
The Department of Rural and Community Development and the 
Gaeltacht (DRCDG), in collaboration with Pobal, hosted a regional 
workshop in Tipperary on 9th July, focused on supporting the delivery 
of the Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme 
(SICAP). The event targeted administrative staff in local authorities 
who provide support to Local Community Development Committees 
(LCDCs) and LCDC members. 
The workshop was chaired by Maria Farry, Manager of the 
Programme Development Unit (SICAP/LEADER), Pobal. Deirdre Kelly, 
Principal Officer, Social Inclusion and Communities Unit (DRCDG) 
delivered a comprehensive overview of SICAP. Her presentation 
outlined:
•	
The programme’s objectives and target groups
•	
Operational 
framework 
and 
interaction 
between 
the 
Department, LCDCs, programme implementers, and Pobal
•	
Contract management roles and responsibilities
•	
Reporting and compliance requirements
Juan Carlos Azzopardi, Development Coordinator with Pobal, 
provided a summary of the programme requirements and timelines. 
He also outlined the supports that are available to LCDC support staff 
and members, an overview of the Annual planning process, including 
financial management and administrative rules around: 
•	
Goal apportionment
•	
Grants and payment instalments
•	
Reporting obligations
The afternoon session included a joint presentation from Bridget 
Fitzgerald, Chief Officer, Kerry Local Community Development 
Committee, and Eamonn O’Reilly, Chief Executive Officer, Northeast 
West Kerry Development on building effective working relationships 
between LCDCs and SICAP programme implementers. Key ingredients 
for successful collaboration included:
•	
Strong and positive engagement at all levels
•	
Capacity to design and deliver tailored responses
•	
Flexible oversight approaches
•	
Responsiveness to community needs
•	
Ability to leverage additional funding streams (e.g., transport, 
literacy, social farming)
They also highlighted ongoing challenges for SICAP including:
•	
Funding & Sustainability: Continued requirement for tendering 
due to EU Procurement Directive; funding levels remain below 
2012 benchmark.
•	
Complex Guidelines: Navigating detailed SICAP guidance.
•	
Targeting Issues: Calls to reassess the use of deprivation indices 
in programme targeting
The workshop concluded with breakout sessions, where participants 
shared recommendations and feedback with the DRCDG to support 
continuous improvement in the delivery and impact of the SICAP 
programme Countrywide.
The official judging for the IPB Pride of Place in Clare
The official judging for the IPB Pride of Place Awards 2025, in 
association with Co-operation Ireland, took place on 8th and 9th July 
2025. Clare County Council nominated four outstanding community 
projects to represent the county in this year’s prestigious all-island 
competition, which celebrates the voluntary efforts of communities 
to improve local well-being, inclusion, sustainability, and pride of 
place.
Over the course of two days, the judges - Brendan McGrath (former 
Chief Executive Galway City) and Declan Nelson (former County 
Manager, Monaghan) visited each of the nominated projects, which 
included presentations, site tours, and engaging discussions with 
community members.
The judges commended the groups for their creativity, commitment, 
and the impressive impact of their work, noting the strong sense of 
community spirit evident throughout the visits.

2
Clare’s Entries for 2025 are:
Creative Community - Obair, Newmarket-on-Fergus
A thriving social enterprise delivering an extensive range of 
community services, including Meals on Wheels, youth support 
programmes, a community crèche, and environmental initiatives. 
Judges toured the impressive facilities and learned about Obair’s 
employment, training, and sustainability projects which underpin 
their ethos of inclusion and resilience.
Population 0-300 - Feakle Community Council
Steeped in tradition and volunteerism, Feakle showcased its vibrant 
community life, with highlights including the care and enhancement 
of the playground and graveyard, a variety of social inclusion 
activities, and the internationally renowned Feakle Traditional Music 
Festival. Judges praised the community’s strong sense of identity and 
pride.
Climate Action & Biodiversity - Inagh Development
An inspiring example of rural climate leadership, Inagh Development 
impressed judges with their innovative and forward-thinking 
projects. These included geothermal and solar energy installations, 
biodiversity enhancements at the church grounds, upgrades to the 
scenic River Walk, and their comprehensive community energy 
masterplan.
	
Community Youth Initiative - Clare Comhairle na nÓg
Young people from Clare Comhairle na nÓg presented their impactful 
“Free Period Products Initiative” and accompanying short film “It 
Should Be Like Toilet Paper.” The judges were deeply impressed 
by their advocacy, creativity, and the practical change they have 
achieved in promoting dignity and equality for young people.
The judges remarked on the calibre of all four entries, noting the 
innovation and passion evident across each community. Their 
positive feedback reflects the ongoing strength and vibrancy of 
Clare’s community development work on the national stage.
The IPB Pride of Place Awards Ceremony 2025 will be held on Friday, 
7th November 2025, at the Limerick Strand Hotel, hosted by Limerick 
City and County Council. The event will also be livestreamed on the 
Pride of Place website.
We extend our congratulations and best wishes to all four nominated 
groups and thank them for representing County Clare with such 
distinction.

Healthy Clare Core Fund
- Clare Garden Festival: Extending the Season 
A total of 15 individuals attended a garending workshop, ‘Autumn 
Gardening for Winter Harvests’, under Clare Growing Communities 
on the 12th August. Supported by Healthy Clare, Clare Garden 
Festival and Clare Local Development Company, the aim is to work 
together with community gardens across Co. Clare assessing support 
needs. The workshop was facilitated by Jo Newton. Of the 15 indi-
vidual who attended the event, all said they they left with skills and 
knowledge to continue growing at home. 
Healthy Clare/Creative Ireland Micro Fund 2025
Clare Walks 
Supported under the Healthy Clare Micro Fund and Creative Ireland 
collaboration, on 14th August, East Clare Walks hosted a Gratitude 
Practice and Self Care Journaling workshop in the Barn Yoga & 
Meditation studio in Killaloe. The workshop started with a talk 
on simple exercises to start a journey to practising Gratitude and 
Journaling. This was followed by a 2 km guided walk in Killaloe where 
participants were encouraged to take photos and notice their sur-
roundings. On 21st August, a Seaweed Foraging talk took place on 
Quilty Beach. Participants were provided with information on differ-
ent types of seaweeds, what they can be used for. Participants were 
also offered the opportunity to take part in a guided walk on Seafield 
Beach. To date over 50 people have taken part in the two events and 
the feedback has been extremely positive.

Clarecare Clay Therapy for Older Adults 
This initiative has been hosted by Clarecare Day Services for Older 
People. These sessions involve individuals working with clay, explor-
ing the range of emotions, thoughts and feelings that come with the 
sensation of working with their hands and moulding shapes that will 
help to bring up joyful memories and support positive mental health. 
For others, the shapes may be a means to support movement and 
dexterity of the hands. The classes focus on the sensory experience 
and how working in a creative manner can help relax the mind.

Association (KBARA)
Funding received from Healthy Clare fund, in partnership with 
Clarisford Park, enabled the group to build a temporary pétanque 
piste. Planning permission to create a permanent facility, complete 
with a piste, fencing, lighting, and seating was granted in June. The 
fund has been instrumental in raising awareness and sparking inter-
est in pétanque within the community. The committee mobilised 
local resources and welcomed the enthusiastic help of up to 14 vol-
unteers, shovels and rakes in hand, to prepare the playing surface. 
Next steps include training members and hosting an Open Day, invit-
ing the wider community to come along, give pétanque a try, and 
share in the enjoyment of this inclusive sport.

Collaboration 
Literacy Proofing to Ensure Use of Plain English 
Healthy Clare and the Limerick and Clare ETB Regional Literacy 
Coordinator worked together to develop a Plain Language version 
of one of their health-related documents, ‘We’re Breastfeeding 
Friendly Clare’. This collaboration ensures that information shared 
with the public is clear, accessible, and easy to understand for all. 
By combining expertise specialist knowledge in the brochure and 
having the information presented in plain language, the partnership 
demonstrates how cross-sector collaboration can lead to practical, 
high-impact outcomes. This initiative highlights the importance of:
•	
Clarity: ensuring health information is written in simple, direct 
language.
•	
Accessibility: making documents more inclusive for people with 
varying literacy levels.
•	
Collaboration: pooling expertise from health services and adult 
literacy support to strengthen communication.
This joint effort stands as a strong example of best practice in 
collaboration, showing how working together can improve public 
engagement, build trust and support healthier communities.

Corofin, North Clare Agricultural Show 
2025: A Joyous Celebration of Rural Life
On Saturday, 26 July 2025, the village of Corofin in North Clare came 
alive with the vibrant sights and sounds of the Corofin, North Clare 
Agricultural Show. The event drew crowds from across the region to 
celebrate the best of local agriculture, horticulture, and community 
spirit.
The show featured a dazzling array of competitions, from prize-
winning vegetables and livestock displays to artisan crafts and 
traditional music. Families, growers, and enthusiasts gathered to 
share knowledge, showcase their talents, and enjoy the warm 
hospitality that Corofin is known for.
The Clare Age Friendly Programme Manager Shanelle Waring was 
delighted to attend, engaging with older members of the community 
and promoting inclusivity and wellbeing throughout the day. 
With perfect weather and a joyful atmosphere, the 2025 show 
was a resounding success—an unforgettable celebration of Clare’s 
agricultural heritage and the people who continue to nurture it.
Ennis West Age Action Group’
Clare Age Friendly Programme Manager, Shanelle Waring, alongside 
the Rural & Community Development Worker Niamh Wiley, recently 
met with members of the newly reformed Ennis West Age Action 
Group. Their visit marked a meaningful step in offering guidance, 
encouragement, and tailored support as the group embarks on a

Clare Age Friendly Attends Successful Seniors 
Information Event in Newmarket-on-Fergus
On Friday, 22nd August 2025, from 1pm to 6pm, the Carrigoran 
Health and Wellness Centre in Newmarket-on-Fergus, Co. Clare, 
hosted a vibrant and well-attended Seniors Information Event. The 
gathering brought together a wide range of community services and 
support organisations; all focused on enhancing the wellbeing and 
independence of older adults.
Clare Age Friendly was delighted to attend and engage with attendees 
throughout the afternoon. The event provided a valuable platform 
for sharing resources, fostering connections, and promoting age-
friendly initiatives across the county.
Visitors had the opportunity to explore health and wellness services, 
receive expert advice, and connect with professionals dedicated 
to supporting older people in Clare. The atmosphere was warm, 
welcoming, and filled with meaningful conversations and community 
spirit. Clare Age Friendly expressed heartfelt thanks to the organisers 
and all involved for their commitment to creating a more inclusive 
and supportive environment for older members of the community.

Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS) 
2024/2025 - Funding Allocations for County Clare
The Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS) provides 
funding for the development, repair, and enhancement of outdoor 
recreational infrastructure, particularly in rural areas across Ireland. 
The scheme supports a wide range of projects aimed at promoting 
outdoor activities and ensuring access to safe, sustainable 
recreational spaces for communities.
On 14 August 2025, Minister Calleary announced €8.7 million for 221 
outdoor recreation projects across the country. The funds allocated 
in this announcement relate to Measure 1 (small scale repair and 
development) and the Project Development Measure. Further 
announcements for Measures 2 and 3 will follow later this year.
Funding Allocation in County Clare:
A total of €278,772 has been awarded to seven projects in County 
Clare, categorised into Measure 1 and the Project Development 
Measure. The funding will support a range of projects designed 
to improve access to outdoor recreational activities, including 
trail development, maintenance, and feasibility studies for future 
outdoor facilities. These investments contribute to both the local 
community’s well-being and the region’s tourism infrastructure.

Local Studies and Archives
Daniel O’Connell 250 with l-r Michael Talty, HelenWalsh, 
Seán Lenihan, Declan Barron, Cathaoirleach 
Paul Murphy and Siobhán Mulcahy.
The Local Studies Centre and Archives have received a donation of 
a Daniel O’Connell letter relating to his duel with John D’Esterre 
in 1815. The letter was sent to his second, Major William Nugent 
MacNamara of Ennistymon. Thanks to Colm Hayes and Frances 
Madigan of the Old Ennistymon Society for the donation. The 
O’Connell 250 Commemoration was held on the 9-10th August, with 
several events being held in the Local Studies and Archives Centre 
in Ennis. An exhibition of books, documents and ephemera relating 
to Daniel O’Connell was held through the month of August. Declan 
Barron (Newpark House) advanced the loan of several documents for 
the exhibition. Lectures by Prof Patrick Geoghegan and Prof Maurice 
Bric were held in DeValera Library and a documentary on O’Connell 
was shown, all events were well-attended. The archiving of John 
Holohan family papers (Feakle Auctioneers and public representa-
tives) is ongoing. The publication “Forgotten Lives” by historian, Rita 
Mc Carthy was launched in the Local Studies section on 21st August 
by Prof Bernadette Whelan, this book tells the story of the County 
Clare Mother and Baby home known as the County Nursery which 
existed from 1922-1932. Over 100 people attended the launch, and 
the highlight of the evening was the address from survivor Jimmy 
King who is now 94 years old. The workhouse was demolished in 
1936.
Clare Museum 
Creative History Camp in Clare Museum 
Two Creative History Summer Camps were held in July with facili-
tator Aideen Sweeney with children aged 6-9 and 10-13. Both 
were fully subscribed and all children enjoyed getting to know the 
Museum artefacts. A Daniel O’Connell exhibition was held as part of 
the O’Connell 250 Commemoration. The museum borrowed items 
from the Newpark House collection for temporary display and digi-
tised three of O’Connell’s letters in the long-term collection, making 
them fully accessible to the public. A blog entry on O’Connell was 
researched and written for the museum website. 
Two events were held during Heritage Week: a drop in informa-
tion morning on Community Archaeology by Archaeologist Tori 
McMorran on 20th August and the launch of the Clare Cillíní Survey 
by Michael Houlihan, held in conjunction with the Heritage Office, 
on 21st August. Over 100 items were catalogued during this period 
and these items will now be photographed and uploaded to the 
website. There were 14 social media posts during the period, pro-
moting museum activities and highlighting aspects of Clare history.
Clare Arts Office 
Súil art gallery welcomed 536 visitors from June 1st - August 12th. Súil

ages 6-9, 10-12, teens and adults, 6 other exhibitions took place in 
Ennis, Scariff and Kilkee.
The “Riches of Clare” concert series took place in glór ever Wednesday 
over the summer, culminating in a performance at Feakle Festival in 
August. Over 1,000 audience members enjoyed music performed by 
36 musicians. “Nourish”, the County Arts Development Plan 2025 
– 2029 was adopted by the Rural Development SPC on 15th July. 
Clare’s “Culture Night” programme was launched which will see with 
over 40 events taking place in 17 towns and villages countywide on 
19th September 2025. Almost 2,000 people attended over 25 events 
in Cultúrlann Sweeney, Kilkee, over the summer months, the busi-
est attendance since COVID. Music, theatre, talks and films had full 
attendance as had art and drama workshop in August.
Almost 500 people attended ‘O’Connell’ in glór, a special com-
missioned theatre and music piece, commemorating the 250th 
anniversary of the birth of Daniel O’Connell. Commissioned by the 
Arts Office and funded by Clare County Council and the Dept of 
Culture, Communications and Sport it was written, produced and 
directed by Diarmuid de Faoite. The Arts Office attended the Film 
Officers AGM at Galway Film Fleadh and assisted with 6 film produc-
tions in Ennis and West Clare over the summer months, 4 arts slots 
took place over the summer on Clare FM and the Arts Officer also 
featured on the Clare FM Roadshow in Mountshannon.

Ballina began on Monday, 28 July 2025 and will continue until 
Friday, 17 October 2025

Local Authority Integration Team 
The Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) have been set up 
in all local authorities. Their purpose is to help coordinate the 
different kinds of support available for people who are applying 
for international protection, refugees, and others in similar 
situations. 
The goal of LAITs is to help IP applicants and refugees become 
independent, settle into their new communities, and participate 
in Irish life. They do this by connecting people to important 
services that can help them integrate into the community. 
Who do LAITs support? 
LAITs provide support for: 
•	 Applicants for International Protection (IP) 
•	 People who have been granted refugee status or other forms 
	
of protection, such as subsidiary protection or permission to 
	
remain 
•	 Refugees who have been resettled in Ireland through a 
	
government programme 
•	 Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs) 
How is the support provided? 
LAITs operate under the principle of 'Integration from Day One'. 
This means that LAITs provide integration support to people 
who need it as soon as they arrive in Ireland. 
What services do LAITs provide? 
The work of LAITs isn’t meant to replace existing services. 
Instead, LAITs help connect people with the existing services 
that are most suitable for their needs. This includes things like: 
•	 Being a direct contact for new arrivals, helping them with 
	
any problems they might have when dealing with public 
	
services 
•	 Connecting new arrivals with services like legal help, 
	
childcare and healthcare 
•	 Connecting new arrivals with services that improve their 
	
ability to live independently, like job training, English classes, 
	
education, and apprenticeships 
•	 Guiding new arrivals through the process of applying for 
	
financial support, medical help, child benefits, and other 
	
services they might need 
•	 Holding meetings in local areas and using community 
	
development principles to help those who attend 
•	 Supporting people if they face racism or other unfair 
	
treatment, helping them report it to the right authorities 
•	 Helping vulnerable new arrivals get in touch with non- 
	
governmental organisations (NGOs) and other services if 
	
they need extra help

ings to maintain and conserve the important structures which form

may receive a maximum grant of €50,000 under the scheme, 
which must represent no more than 80% of the project’s total cost. 
Buildings/structures eligible for funding under the scheme include:

of protected structures)
•	
Proposed protected structures (i.e. buildings the local author-
ity has proposed to add to its list)
•	
Structures in Architectural Conservation Areas (ACAs are

Investment Grade Audit for the Aras
Tipperary Energy Agency (TEA) has for the past year been car-
rying out a detailed energy survey known as an Investment 
Grade Audit on council headquarters at the Aras. This audit was 
conducted under an EU funded project dubbed Transforming 
Renovation in the Atlantic Seaboard South (TRESS). The pur-
pose behind TRESS is to create a prioritisation framework for 
retrofitting buildings in the southwest region of Ireland to assist 
public bodies in developing pathways to meet decarbonisation 
and energy efficiency targets.
Staff from TEA visited the offices of Clare County Council on 7th 
August to present the culmination of their 12 month deep dive 
energy audit to members of the Facilities and Energy teams. 
While being very complimentary about the way existing plant 
and equipment is used and maintained by the Facilities team, 
the Investment Grade Audit has highlighted potential decar-
bonisation and energy efficiency measures that may be imple-
mented to accelerate our drive to meet nationally binding tar-
gets. The detailed analysis and options presented for heating 
the Aras into the future will forearm the Energy team as we en-
ter the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) National 
Building Retrofit Pathfinder Programme wherein matched fund-
ing will be made available for major energy retrofit projects at 
the Aras and Ennis Leisure Centre.

experienced clinicians provided by St Gabriel’s and supported 
in their academic training by the School of Allied Health at UL. 
HAPPEE benefits the community by supporting the early iden-
tification of needs in schools whilst also creating much needed 
sustainable student placements for the University.
